Scope warning. This is a preprint and benchmark study. It supports claims about the tested models, benchmark splits, route-search procedure, and measured costs; it does not establish deployment robustness, universal model-family generalization, or per-input dynamic routing.

One-page synthesis

Core thesis. A frozen transformer can sometimes be made more accurate by changing the order in which its existing blocks are executed. MACRO learns a task-level probability distribution over routes that can skip, repeat, revisit, add prior hidden states, or rejoin the standard suffix; it then uses exact top-k Viterbi decoding plus held-out validation to choose one deterministic route for test-time use.

What the paper reports. Averaged over six shared model settings, MACRO improves accuracy by about +5.0 points over the ordinary forward pass, by +7.2 points over Dr.LLM, and by +1.5 points over Dr.LLM when Dr.LLM is given MACRO's extended action space. Route-search time is reported as 1.6 h vs 14.8 h per benchmark for MACRO versus Dr.LLM, a 9.4× reduction. Gains are highly heterogeneous: Qwen3-1.7B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B gain roughly 13 points on average, while stronger Qwen models gain under 2 points and Llama-3.2-3B gains only 0.33 points in the appendix.

Why it matters. The work treats transformer depth as a programmable computation graph rather than a fixed sequence, while keeping model weights frozen and avoiding per-example test-time route search. The strongest design idea is not simply “skip layers”: the action space, constrained Markov policy, exact top-k decoder, and validation-based route selection all matter. The results suggest that some model errors can be changed by re-exposing or preserving internal information through a different sequence of frozen blocks.

Primary limits. The method still requires labeled training/validation feedback to learn each task route; “No Labels” in the paper means no test labels. Final inference uses one fixed route per task, not an input-conditioned router. External validation is limited to transfer among the same benchmark family, contamination checks are not reported, mechanistic evidence is limited, and the measured Qwen3-1.7B inference tradeoff is about +16.1% latency and +4.6% peak GPU memory on a single A40.

Source map

Introduction & related work

The source positions MACRO against early-exit/layer-dropping methods, CoLA, Dr.LLM, Neuroanatomy, recurrent-depth models, and mixture-of-experts approaches. Its objective differs from speed-oriented adaptive depth: it searches for alternate frozen-layer programs specifically to improve task accuracy.

The motivating example is Qwen3-1.7B on GSM8K: a route that executes L0–L7, rewinds to L3, and then continues forward raises a reported test result from 43.44% to 69.52%, while increasing block calls from 28 to 33.

Method

MACRO represents routing as a context-dependent Markov policy over a typed program. State factors are current layer, budget phase, incoming layer displacement, and operator context. Actions are local layer moves, add-and-apply operations using an earlier hidden state, and Rejoin to the standard suffix. Feasibility masks prevent out-of-range or over-budget programs.

The policy starts from a forward-biased prior and is updated by an estimation-of-distribution / cross-entropy-method-like procedure using route accuracy on training chunks plus a replay buffer. After search, exact top-k Viterbi decoding yields the most probable valid route programs; a held-out validation set selects the final route.

Experiments & appendices

The main suite spans 13 reasoning/knowledge benchmarks across Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B, 4-bit Qwen3-14B, 4-bit Mixtral-8x7B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B; Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct appears in Appendix A. Baselines include the normal forward pass, Dr.LLM, Dr.LLM with MACRO's extended action space, MACRO without Viterbi, and MACRO top-1 without validation selection.

Appendices provide selected routes, a one-model-one-route transfer experiment, selected-action frequencies, search hyperparameters, exactness details for top-k decoding, and an inference-cost profile.

Methods

Problem formulation

For a pretrained transformer with frozen blocks f1…fL, a route is a program over those blocks. The optimization target is route accuracy on labeled data:

r* = argmax_r Acc(r)
Acc(r) = (1/N) Σ_i 1{ M_r(x_i) = y_i }

The dataset is split into disjoint train, validation, and test components. Training data are further divided across search rounds; each round evaluates candidates on a fresh chunk plus a replay buffer drawn from earlier chunks.

State and action space

ComponentSource definitionFunctional role
Current layer ℓMost recently produced layerAnchors feasible next layer operations.
Budget phase φearly / mid / lateConditions behavior on remaining route-length budget; strongly supported by ablation.
Incoming displacement δSigned gap from prior layer plus start symbolPreserves local movement context for exact decoding.
Operator context oPlain layer vs add-produced stateConditions future actions on operation provenance.
Local moveMove within radius rSupports skips, repeats, and backward revisits.
Add-and-applyForm ht + γht-b, then apply a local destination layerIntroduces residual reuse of earlier hidden state.
RejoinTerminate learned prefix and execute normal remaining suffixProvides a deterministic path back to the base network.

Search and final selection

The main experiments use 10 search iterations with 30 sampled programs per iteration, replay fraction 0.1, local radius r=5, six-state history for add actions, γ=1.0, εloc=0.2, εop=0.0867, smoothing α=0.0397, selection sharpness β=1.8262, and an elite set of five programs. Search stops early when all sampled programs become semantically identical after Rejoin expansion.

Each run requests 1,000 training examples and a held-out validation split (100 examples in standard runs, 200 in baseline-anchored 4-bit/non-Qwen runs; smaller pools are split proportionally). Seeds are (1, 2, 42). Generation is greedy with temperature 0, top-p 1.0, top-k 0, ≤400 thinking tokens, and ≤128 answer tokens. Final candidate sets use top-5 Viterbi for Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B and Llama-3.2-3B; baseline + four nonstandard Viterbi neighbors for Qwen3-14B, Mixtral, and DeepSeek.

Methodological strength. The train/validation/test separation, exact final decoding, explicit feasibility constraints, seeded repeats, action-space control baseline (Dr.LLM+Ext.), ablations, and benchmark-level significance analysis make the central claim substantially stronger than a single-route demo.

Main results

Table 2 reports model-by-benchmark accuracy. The average over these six shared model settings is approximately 63.68 → 68.69 (+5.01 points). The corresponding mean model-average for Dr.LLM is approximately 61.49, making MACRO +7.20 points higher; Dr.LLM+Ext. averages approximately 67.20, leaving MACRO +1.49 points higher. This decomposition supports the authors' argument that the richer action space itself explains part, but not all, of the benefit.

Important heterogeneity. Full MACRO is not the strongest method on every model. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, Dr.LLM+Ext. averages 62.53 versus 55.91 for MACRO, and Dr.LLM averages 58.62. The paper explicitly notes that MACRO has the best mean accuracy on every tested main model except the reasoning-distilled one.

Viterbi and validation selection

MACRO without Viterbi deploys the best route sampled during training; MACRO top-1 uses the most probable Viterbi route but skips held-out validation selection. Full MACRO is strongest on four of six main models and on the overall average, supporting both decoding and validation selection as useful safeguards against a lucky sampled route or an over-probable but suboptimal route.

Transfer, mechanistic evidence, and cost

Mechanistic interpretability

A logit-lens analysis on Qwen3-1.7B tracks the correct-answer token through depth. In the four shown tasks, the standard route sometimes carries a stronger correct-answer signal internally and then suppresses it near the output; the MACRO route preserves a higher final signal. The paper reports endpoint log-probability advantages of +15.4 (SVAMP), +14.0 (OpenBookQA), +9.8 (GSM8K), and +7.5 (MATH500).

Interpretation boundary. This is suggestive, not causal. The analysis is limited to one model and four examples/benchmark traces, and it cannot by itself establish that MACRO generally “recovers an already-computed answer” rather than changing intermediate computation in other ways.

One model, one route

A shared route trained over eight in-domain tasks improves Qwen3-1.7B from 71.50 to 74.29 in-domain (+2.79) and from 30.98 to 40.00 out-of-domain (+9.02). For Qwen3-4B, the shared-route gains are much smaller: +0.30 in-domain and +1.12 out-of-domain. Individual out-of-domain cells can decline; for Qwen3-4B, the shared route is -0.88 on GSM8K, -0.13 on MMLU-Pro, and -4.27 on MedQA.

Route transfer matrix

Cross-benchmark route transfer is mostly strongest on the diagonal, with off-diagonal benefits concentrated among related math tasks. This supports partial reuse of route structure but also reinforces that the current method is substantially task-specific.

Inference cost

On Qwen3-1.7B, the Appendix D profile uses 64 test items per benchmark, a two-stage 400/128-token greedy budget, and a single A40. Across 13 benchmarks, the reported mean overhead is +16.1% latency and +4.6% peak GPU memory (335 MB). Some routes are faster or lighter than baseline when they execute fewer blocks, but the average route is more expensive.

Exactness of top-k decoding

The paper emphasizes that top-k decoding is exact rather than beam-like. Because future transitions depend on incoming displacement and operator context, the dynamic program uses an augmented state keyed on current layer, budget phase, incoming delta, operator context, previous layer, and length. Program length increases monotonically, yielding a finite DAG; retaining the k best continuations per state yields the exact global top-k under the learned masked policy.

Figure D.1 — Inference-time cost (p. 16). Qwen3-1.7B, single A40, 64 test items per benchmark. Mean route overhead: +16.1% latency and +4.6% / 335 MB peak memory. Representation: embedded crop.

Evaluation and appraisal

Verdict: Read first. The paper is unusually relevant for work on small-model capability, test-time compute, and parameter-frozen adaptation. It is methodologically substantial enough to merit close reading, but the current evidence supports “promising benchmark method” more strongly than “general-purpose inference improvement.”
Relevance
9/10

Rationale: Directly addresses inference-time computation structure and small-model capability without weight updates.

Evidence: Multiple model families, reasoning/knowledge tasks, quantized settings, latency/memory profile.

Limit: Static task routes rather than input-adaptive routing.

Would raise: Per-input routing with similarly low search/training burden.

Novelty
8/10

Rationale: Combines constrained Markov routing, residual hidden-state add operations, exact top-k decoding, and validation selection in a distinctive frozen-model framework.

Evidence: Direct comparison with Dr.LLM, CoLA/Neuroanatomy positioning, Dr.LLM+Ext. control.

Limit: Builds on recurrent depth, adaptive depth, CEM, and routing precedents.

Would raise: Demonstrated input-conditioned routing or stronger mechanistic theory.

Method strength
8/10

Rationale: Clear split discipline, ablations, controlled action-space comparison, exact decoder, three seeds, statistical testing.

Evidence: Tables 2–4, Appendix C, route catalog.

Limit: Benchmark-only study; no independent replication or contamination analysis reported.

Would raise: External replication, contamination checks, broader compute accounting.

Evidence strength
7/10

Rationale: Main accuracy claim is supported across many model–benchmark cells and benchmark-level statistics.

Evidence: Significant positive model-level benchmark shifts; strong small-model gains; ablations.

Limit: Gains are heterogeneous; some comparison methods beat MACRO on DeepSeek; common benchmarks may not represent deployment behavior.

Would raise: Fresh external tasks, independent evaluation, prospective deployment-style workloads.

External validity
6/10

Rationale: Multiple architectures and tasks help, but generalization is still mostly within standard benchmark ecosystems.

Evidence: Qwen, Mixtral, DeepSeek, Llama; cross-benchmark route transfer.

Limit: Transfer is mostly diagonal/task-specific and shared routes can hurt individual tasks.

Would raise: New domains, unseen datasets, larger model families, different quantization/hardware stacks.

Implementation value
8/10

Rationale: The algorithm is concrete, hyperparameters and route notation are reported, and the source reports public code.

Evidence: Appendix B/C, exact Viterbi description, cost appendix.

Limit: Task-specific labeled search and custom layer/cache execution are nontrivial.

Would raise: End-to-end packaged support across common inference engines and consumer hardware benchmarks.

Main strengths

  • Strong experimental decomposition separates action-space effects from the routing optimizer.
  • Test data are held out from route search and final validation selection.
  • Exact top-k decoding is carefully justified rather than described as a generic beam search.
  • Statistical analysis uses benchmark-level differences rather than treating seed replicates as independent.
  • Appendices expose route strings, candidate rules, hyperparameters, and inference overhead.

Main limitations / red flags to keep in view

  • Not label-free: training and validation labels are used to optimize route accuracy; only test-label use is avoided.
  • Not input-dynamic at inference: the deployed route is one task-level program. The paper's future direction explicitly calls for more extensive input-dependent routing.
  • Benchmark contamination not assessed: the paper does not report contamination or memorization checks for the pretrained models on these public datasets.
  • Generalization is mixed: route-transfer heatmaps are mostly diagonal and shared routes produce some negative task deltas.
  • Hardware/cost evidence is narrow: detailed inference profiling is only shown for Qwen3-1.7B on a single A40; route-search cost comparison lacks a similarly complete hardware-normalized breakdown in the paper.
  • Mechanistic claim is preliminary: logit-lens evidence is suggestive but limited and not causal.
  • Effect size compresses on stronger models: Qwen3-4B/8B/14B gains are modest, and Llama-3.2-3B is nearly unchanged on average.
Do not overclaim. The paper does not show that arbitrary LLMs have a universally better hidden route, that MACRO is “free” accuracy, or that the learned route transfers safely across tasks. It demonstrates that a constrained offline search can often find task-level alternate layer programs that improve benchmark accuracy for the tested frozen models.

Implementation / research takeaways

1. Treat depth as a program. Layer order can be a search space, not just a fixed architecture. Skips alone are insufficient; repeats, backward moves, residual reuse, and a safe rejoin operator are useful primitives.
2. Search globally, deploy deterministically. MACRO's practical pattern is offline exploration → compact probabilistic policy → exact candidate decoding → validation selection → one fixed deployment route.
3. Preserve a baseline floor. Baseline-anchored candidate sets for 4-bit/non-Qwen runs are a useful safety pattern: keep the standard route available and select a nonstandard route only when validation supports it.
4. Action space matters as much as optimizer. Dr.LLM+Ext. substantially closes the gap to MACRO. Any replication should treat routing primitives as a first-class experimental variable.
5. Small/weak models are the highest-value target. The largest average gains occur on Qwen3-1.7B and the distilled DeepSeek model; stronger Qwen models show much smaller gains.
6. Budget for inference overhead. Accuracy gains often come from longer routes. A prototype should track executed block count, latency, KV-cache depth, and memory, not only benchmark accuracy.

Good prototype question

A useful replication would ask: Can a small open-weight model gain on a narrow, labeled task by searching a restricted skip/repeat/rejoin route space, and does the gain survive a fresh held-out dataset while staying within a fixed latency budget? Starting without hidden-state add operations would simplify implementation; add them only after establishing a route-search baseline.
